claims.claim_text: Backing is a pledge rather than a purchase: a card is registered at the time of backing and charged only if the campaign reaches its stated goal, so an unfunded project costs its backers nothing.
claims.quote_verbatim: if they don't meet their goal, then you get it all back
claims.episode_title: 555 Contest, Computer Museum, Octopart - The Green Pen Hornswoggle

claims.claim_text: Roughly eight to nine percent of the raised total is taken before the creator sees it, five percent to the platform and three to five percent to the payment processor.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's 5% Kickstarter plus 3 to 5% payment processor
claims.episode_title: An Interview with David Kronstein (Tesla500)

claims.claim_text: Further money never arrives at all, because a proportion of pledged cards decline or fail in the interval between pledging and collection, and a reserve must be left with the processor against chargebacks; the headline campaign total is therefore an overstatement of what is available to spend.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's a certain amount of people's, like, their credit cards were maxed
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Intense Illusion Introduction

claims.claim_text: Funds arrive only after the campaign closes and a further holding period, so parts must be ordered against the creator's own money if delivery is not to start weeks late. Platforms that release funds as soon as the target is met remove that gap, and the difference in payout timing is a substantive reason projects run late.
claims.quote_verbatim: you've got to wait until the campaign ends. Then you've got to wait two weeks
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Chris Becomes Self Employed - Quixotic Quitting Quaere

claims.claim_text: Long-lead components must be committed to before the campaign even launches if the promised delivery date is to be met, so a creator is exposed for thousands of dollars before any money is raised.
claims.quote_verbatim: I just paid 4,200 bucks for a reel of bloody components
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Andrew Witte - Telistic Timepiece Technomania

claims.claim_text: The platform originally had no mechanism for collecting shipping addresses, only a single one-time survey, so a campaign with tens of thousands of backers had to build its own web application to gather and correct addresses.
claims.quote_verbatim: Kickstarter didn't even have a mailing address feature
claims.speaker: Andrew Witte
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Andrew Witte - Telistic Timepiece Technomania

claims.claim_text: The backer survey can be sent only once, so an error in it or a wrong address supplied by a backer cannot be corrected through the platform. Its export is otherwise usable: results download repeatedly as a spreadsheet, sortable by reward level and by whether an item has shipped.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can only run it once
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Manufacturing By Wire And Skipping Testing - Calefacient Cuculine Cash

claims.claim_text: Several campaign parameters, including the receiving bank details, are fixed at launch and cannot be changed afterwards.
claims.quote_verbatim: they can't change your bank details after you launch the campaign
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Discussing Innovation and the Future with Mike Ossmann - Fiesty Festivus Futurology

claims.claim_text: Only backers can comment on a campaign, so posting a public objection on a project's own page costs the price of the smallest pledge.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can't leave a comment on the Kickstarter site
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Mars, Makerbot & Power Outages - Reprobate Replicator Replication

claims.claim_text: Campaign creation was restricted by country for years, tied to the payment processor, so creators outside the permitted countries needed a partner resident in one to take legal responsibility for the campaign.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're Australian, you can't do it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - The Ternary Tussle

claims.claim_text: Regional crowdfunding platforms existed but did not substitute, because the value of the largest platform is the audience already browsing it for projects to fund; a campaign hosted anywhere else is closer to selling from one's own website.
claims.quote_verbatim: the whole purpose of being on Kickstarter is that you're on Kickstarter
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Proemial Passive Poiesis

claims.claim_text: The platform's public position, stated after non-delivery complaints, was that backing a project is not buying a product. Rules introduced at the same time required creators to answer what risks and challenges the project faced and what qualified them to overcome them.
claims.quote_verbatim: the title of their post was, Kickstarter is not a store
claims.episode_title: Kickstarter, Manufacturing, Open Hardware - Judging Jurisdictional Junctures

claims.claim_text: A working prototype became mandatory, ending campaigns built on renderings alone; projects unable to meet that bar moved to platforms without it.
claims.quote_verbatim: Kickstarter have new rules that say you must show a real working prototype
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Kickstarter, IndieGoGo & Ignite - Jasperated Jimswinger Jobbery

claims.claim_text: The prototype rule has been enforced retroactively against large campaigns: one project was suspended after raising about four million dollars, having reached the top tier of funding on the site, on the ground that it had no working prototype.
claims.quote_verbatim: They suspended it based on the fact that it didn't have a working prototype
claims.episode_title: Amazon Moves In, Dave Says Run

claims.claim_text: The prototype rule leaves the substantive question open, since a project's stated purpose is usually to fund the work of making an impractical demonstration practical, and no definition settles how closely the prototype must match the claims.
claims.quote_verbatim: Does a prototype have to perform as good as your claims?
claims.episode_title: Amazon Moves In, Dave Says Run

claims.claim_text: Hardware campaigns undergo more review before approval than other categories, with a nominal approval time of about a week.
claims.quote_verbatim: the hardware ones are subjected to more scrutiny than the regular ones
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Funding New/Manufacturing Old Projects - Radical Robotic Requisition

claims.claim_text: Review does not scale with volume: a campaign explicitly claiming perpetual motion and infinite energy was reported and returned as not violating any guideline, indicating that reviewers work a checklist of required elements rather than assessing physical plausibility.
claims.quote_verbatim: it doesn't violate any of our guidelines
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Use The Protection Circuit

claims.claim_text: Whole product categories are excluded by rules that are not obvious in advance, and campaigns have been rejected under criteria the creators did not know applied to them.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can't put home improvement devices on Kickstarter
claims.speaker: Andrew Witte
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Andrew Witte - Telistic Timepiece Technomania

claims.claim_text: The terms require a creator who cannot deliver to make a good-faith effort to refund, but the obligation is contractual rather than practically enforceable, and by the time a project fails the money has usually been spent.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you cannot deliver your promise rewards, you will do your best to refund people their money
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Our Second Callin Show(ish)

claims.claim_text: The refund requirement collides with the sequence of events: money is spent on tooling and parts before the shortfall becomes apparent, so a project in trouble has neither the product nor the funds.
claims.quote_verbatim: But at that stage, they've spent the money and it's very difficult to give it back
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: Refunds also become mechanically difficult with time, since payment systems stop allowing a transaction to be reversed after a period, leaving individual repayment as the only route.
claims.quote_verbatim: PayPal only allow you to do a refund after a certain amount of time
claims.speaker: Jeff Rowberg
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeff Rowberg - Mini Module Master

claims.claim_text: The pledge curve has a characteristic shape: a large surge in the first days from people already watching the platform, a long flat middle, and a rise at the deadline. Press coverage during the middle produces only small blips, and adjusting the campaign's presentation does not lift it off the floor.
claims.quote_verbatim: once the people pile through the first couple of days, they never come back
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Intense Illusion Introduction

claims.claim_text: Third-party tools that extrapolate a campaign's final total from its current rate are misleading precisely because the curve decays: an early projection can be an order of magnitude above the outcome.
claims.quote_verbatim: day one, when everything was going really well, it was something like $10 million
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Intense Illusion Introduction

claims.claim_text: One of the strongest predictors of a campaign's outcome is the size of the audience the creator already has, which makes audience building part of the engineering project rather than something separable from it.
claims.quote_verbatim: one of the main factors is how many followers do you have on Facebook
claims.episode_title: Google Glass, Lean Startup and VotC - Initializing Instructed Interviews

claims.claim_text: About a third of pledges come from repeat backers, who arrive after a campaign has visible momentum rather than creating it; the observed failure rate rises sharply for projects that attract almost no backers at launch.
claims.quote_verbatim: a third of our pledges are coming from repeat backers
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Zach Dunham

claims.claim_text: The conventional sequence is grassroots outreach to friends, family and interested parties, then a mailing list, then launch, so that the campaign opens with momentum the platform's own audience can then amplify. A campaign posted and left alone is the failure case.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're doing some amount of grassroots outreach, friends, family growing out from their influencers, building a mailing list
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Zach Dunham

claims.claim_text: No large campaign has succeeded on the merits of the idea alone; each had a deliberate outreach effort behind it, whether or not anyone on the team was called a marketer.
claims.quote_verbatim: even the best Kickstarter projects have not been like that
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Zach Dunham

claims.claim_text: Press activity during a campaign is scheduled at a rate that is itself a full-time job, in one case three interviews or appearances a day in the first week, dropping to two a week and then one a day, on top of a backer correspondence load that does not decline.
claims.quote_verbatim: the first week was three things a day
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Intense Illusion Introduction

claims.claim_text: Crowdfunding does three separable things: it moves money from the point of sale back to the point where design and parts must be paid for, it performs market research on whether the product is wanted, and it assembles a community with a stake in the outcome. A project that already has money and a community is buying only the market research.
claims.quote_verbatim: it basically moves money forward in time
claims.speaker: Chris Anderson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chris Anderson - Deambulatory Daedal Drones

claims.claim_text: The cost of the model is the commitment it creates: backers reasonably feel they have bought the product described, so the ordinary development practice of changing direction as the design teaches you something reads as a bait and switch.
claims.quote_verbatim: I kind of reserve the right to change gears
claims.speaker: Chris Anderson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chris Anderson - Deambulatory Daedal Drones

claims.claim_text: An unsuccessful campaign is a cheap negative result: if the interest does not exist, nothing happens and no inventory was built. That property is a large part of the model's value to a small hardware project.
claims.quote_verbatim: it is built in market research
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Interview with Michael Ossmann - Gifted Grimgribber Grokker

claims.claim_text: Where prototypes and small runs can be bought for a few hundred dollars, the funding function matters much less than the publicity, so the reason for running a campaign shifts from capital to attention.
claims.quote_verbatim: What you need Kickstarter for is for the publicity
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: The Art Of Staying Interested In Electronics - Exponible Electronics Ennui

claims.claim_text: A creator who already has an audience can take pre-orders from their own site to the same effect; the platform's distinct value is to someone with no audience, who gets access to people browsing for projects to fund.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's nerds just sitting on Kickstarter
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Mars, Makerbot & Power Outages - Reprobate Replicator Replication

claims.claim_text: A completed campaign functions as evidence for later investors in a way a plan cannot: working hardware plus people who have already paid for it converts a pitch from a claim about the future into a demonstrated fact.
claims.quote_verbatim: until you have something to physically show people, you're just another smart person with an ambitious plan
claims.speaker: Luke Iseman
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Luke Iseman of yCombinator

claims.claim_text: The same evidence works with institutions unfamiliar with crowdfunding: the transaction record of campaign proceeds arriving is documentary proof of where a business's money came from.
claims.quote_verbatim: I had a proof in the form of the Kickstarter campaign
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Only A Transmitter

claims.claim_text: Backers are not investors and receive no equity; offering equity in exchange for a pledge would be a securities matter and is a persistent misunderstanding among people new to the model.
claims.quote_verbatim: they think when there's Kickstarter involved, they're like, oh, so I get a piece of the company
claims.episode_title: An interview with Ariel Briner of Cartesian Co

claims.claim_text: Crowdfunding was chosen over an accelerator or investment because the transaction is bounded: a defined product delivered for a defined sum, with no continuing claim on whatever the founders do afterwards.
claims.quote_verbatim: There's none of this ambiguous 7% stake in whatever you might do for the rest of your life
claims.speaker: Ian Daniher
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ian Daniher - Nascent Nonolith Numquid

claims.claim_text: The most common failure pattern is a team that reaches the last stretch of development, is funded well beyond its goal, and has no idea what to do next, because the remaining work is manufacturing rather than design.
claims.quote_verbatim: get funded way beyond their goals, and then have no clue what to do beyond that
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: Underpricing is endemic: campaigns are priced without accounting for cost of goods, tooling and non-recurring engineering, so a creator can raise half a million dollars and still make nothing, having left no margin.
claims.quote_verbatim: they just didn't understand the cost of goods and the overhead manufacturing costs from tools, NRE
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: Backers will not fund a realistic two-year schedule, so campaigns promise delivery in months. Combining an unrealistic schedule with first-time volume manufacturing, direct customer contact and an inadequate budget describes most of the failures.
claims.quote_verbatim: you have to set some reasonable delivery date
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: Lateness is the norm rather than the exception, and it follows structurally from having to commit to a delivery date before the decisions that determine the schedule, such as who will be hired to do the work, can be made.
claims.quote_verbatim: 80% of Kickstarter campaigns are late
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Absorptive Augmented Actuality

claims.claim_text: For a given product there is a price and volume combination below which the campaign cannot succeed regardless of effort: at a low enough unit price, a creator paying themselves and their helpers nothing still runs out of money before delivery. Stretch goals move a campaign in the wrong direction on that curve.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's this viability curve, and if you're under the viability curve, you are guaranteed to go bankrupt
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Wrong Hardware, Wrong Software - Fugacious Fan Funding

claims.claim_text: Outcomes divide into three bands. A small campaign that barely funds is a manageable side project; a very large one funds a full-time company. The middle band is the difficult one, where there is too much work to do alone and not enough money to hire anyone to help.
claims.quote_verbatim: he called the middle one the pit of despair
claims.episode_title: Ceramic capacitors & High end scopes - Kempt Kickstarter Kakorrhaphiophobia

claims.claim_text: Almost all of a campaign's proceeds are already committed to building what was promised, so the sum arriving in the account bears no relation to what the creator has earned.
claims.quote_verbatim: half a million dollars suddenly appears in your bank account and you feel rich and then you realize
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Ludicrously High Frequency Interference

claims.claim_text: Even a campaign raising several hundred thousand dollars from a few thousand backers can leave its creator unable to say whether it was profitable once building, testing, shipping and supporting the units are counted, and it is likely to be poor against an hourly rate.
claims.quote_verbatim: how much profit did I make in the end from that? I don't know
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Your Mind Is The Tool

claims.claim_text: Cash management, not technical failure, is the usual proximate cause of a funded project collapsing.
claims.quote_verbatim: this is a reason a lot of Kickstarters go out of business, you know? Right. Poor cash management
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Cash Is King

claims.claim_text: Over-funding must be planned for as carefully as under-funding: a campaign that raises several times its goal has committed its creator to several times the work at the same margin, and success at that scale is itself the hazard.
claims.quote_verbatim: plan for getting more money than you asked for
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bart Dring

claims.claim_text: Asking for a fixed sum in exchange for a fixed reward price removes any later opportunity to correct the numbers, so the price must carry a buffer; the advice given repeatedly to first-time creators is to double it.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're building in some, some buffer
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Zach Dunham

claims.claim_text: Capping the number of units a campaign will sell bounds the manufacturing commitment deliberately: the purpose of the campaign is to get the project off the ground, and any quantity beyond that adds risk and strains the assembly partner without changing the outcome.
claims.quote_verbatim: It just reduces risk
claims.speaker: Marcus Schappi
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Marcus Schappi - Kit Ketch Kenophobia

claims.claim_text: Orders with a new manufacturer are escalated in stages: a small pre-production run built by exactly the methods intended for volume, evaluated, then a larger order, then larger again as confidence in the supplier's process accumulates. The failure this avoids is opening ten thousand boxes to find every unit damaged, as happened when a run of finished products was scratched by the racking used to store the boards.
claims.quote_verbatim: I just want 50 units that are manufactured using the exact same methods
claims.speaker: Simone Giertz
claims.episode_title: Product Design with Simone Giertz

claims.claim_text: A planned pre-campaign lot of forty units for field feedback was overtaken by schedule pressure, so the first several hundred campaign units became the test lot instead. The magnitude of the exposure changes by an order of magnitude when that step is skipped.
claims.quote_verbatim: the first 450 will be the test lot
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Debugger vs Printeffer

claims.claim_text: Contract manufacturers offer end-to-end campaign fulfilment covering sourcing, assembly, programming, test and shipping, with the test fixture either supplied by the customer or designed for a fee, because a defective product reflects on the assembler as well as the creator.
claims.quote_verbatim: We actually do end to end Kickstarter services
claims.speaker: Chris Church
claims.episode_title: An interview with Macrofab - Macro Manufacturing Mechanization

claims.claim_text: The platform eventually partnered with distributors and manufacturing consultancies on a programme intended to reduce hardware failure rates, providing manufacturing guidance to selected projects.
claims.quote_verbatim: Kickstarter is launching a program to help prevent hardware startups from failing
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Milling About

claims.claim_text: That programme is curated and requires a previous successful campaign, so it is closed to exactly the first-time creators whose failure rate motivated it. Its practical target is projects already prototyped and close to manufacturable.
claims.quote_verbatim: you need to have a previous successful Kickstarter
claims.episode_title: Mergers and People Acquisitions

claims.claim_text: A live campaign attracts a stream of service providers offering fulfilment, manufacturing or survey handling in exchange for a percentage of the raise, some of them researching the creator individually to make the approach personal.
claims.quote_verbatim: all the vultures, you start getting all these emails
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Discussing Innovation and the Future with Mike Ossmann - Fiesty Festivus Futurology

claims.claim_text: The recommended preparation for running a campaign is to back a number of small projects first and follow their updates from the backer's side, then ask creators who have run one what they know now that they did not know then.
claims.quote_verbatim: Spend $10, back 10 different projects for a buck
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Zach Dunham

claims.claim_text: A creator cannot prove in advance that manufacturing will go well, since even experienced teams fail; documenting the process publicly as it happens is the closest available substitute, and openness correlates with lower risk.
claims.quote_verbatim: the most open projects are the lowest risk probably
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Zach Dunham

claims.claim_text: Backers frequently cannot distinguish a proof of concept from a looks-like or works-like prototype or a production-ready design, so creators are encouraged to state explicitly which stage they are at; even a project in final production can still fail.
claims.quote_verbatim: clearly communicate the stage
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Zach Dunham

claims.claim_text: For products whose function is easy to fake in a video, an unedited demonstration filmed in full from multiple angles is the practical verification, which is why some categories are asked for it.
claims.quote_verbatim: a full, full length print and unedited video on camera from multiple angles
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Zach Dunham

claims.claim_text: The main competing platform offers flexible funding, where the creator keeps whatever is raised whether or not the target is met, alongside an all-or-nothing option. It also predates the larger platform and applies looser rules, which makes it the destination for projects rejected elsewhere.
claims.quote_verbatim: you get the money regardless of whether or not you meet the target
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Kickstarter, IndieGoGo & Ignite - Jasperated Jimswinger Jobbery

claims.claim_text: A curated platform for open hardware treats the campaign as a product launch rather than a funding event: it selects the projects it works with, provides fulfilment and marketing, and then continues to stock and sell the product afterwards, so delivery is the start of the relationship rather than its end.
claims.quote_verbatim: Delivery is the beginning for us
claims.speaker: Josh Lifton
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Josh Lifton

claims.claim_text: That platform was founded in direct response to the non-delivery problem and to the larger platform's public position that it was not a store, by people who had built products themselves and could see what was coming.
claims.quote_verbatim: that was really the catalyst
claims.speaker: Josh Lifton
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Josh Lifton

claims.claim_text: Running the same campaign simultaneously on two platforms became standard practice, which increases reach and correspondingly increases the number of backers exposed if the project fails.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's always dual platform, usually at the same time
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Bill and Dave's Excellent Equipment

claims.claim_text: Crowdfunding audiences do not transfer between platforms: the smaller ones lack the numbers and the flow of high-profile projects, so the choice of platform materially changes the amount raised for the same project.
claims.quote_verbatim: they don't have the same audience. They don't have the same numbers
claims.speaker: Ian Daniher
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ian Daniher - Nascent Nonolith Numquid

claims.claim_text: A smartwatch campaign asked for one hundred thousand dollars, enough for roughly a thousand watches, and raised about ten million from tens of thousands of backers, converting a build that could almost have been done by hand into a mass-production programme overseas.
claims.quote_verbatim: You ended up getting 10 million bucks
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Andrew Witte - Telistic Timepiece Technomania

claims.claim_text: A successful hardware campaign need not be large: about 441 backers and fifty-odd thousand dollars against a sixteen thousand dollar goal was enough to make manufacture worthwhile, and continuing sales after the campaign were what let its creator leave employment.
claims.quote_verbatim: you raised $50,000, $53,000 of your $16,000 goal, but it's only 441 backers
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Interview with Michael Ossmann - Gifted Grimgribber Grokker

claims.claim_text: A campaign for a measurement instrument aimed at six thousand dollars, enough for a first board run, and tripled it after coverage on hardware blogs and interest from the educational market, taking the team from proof of concept and rendered mock-up through a production run of a few hundred units.
claims.quote_verbatim: we wound up tripling our goal
claims.speaker: Ian Daniher
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ian Daniher - Nascent Nonolith Numquid

claims.claim_text: An augmented-reality campaign raising just over a million dollars from about three thousand backers was the company's first outside money and funded its first hires, with the team still working from a house.
claims.quote_verbatim: we raised a bit over a million dollars and had, like, 3,000 backers
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: Jeri Ellsworth and the demise of CastAR

claims.claim_text: Campaign-era hardware should not be shown to investors once better prototypes exist: a series B pitch made with the crowdfunded units, which most of those investors had already seen, exhausted the single opportunity each firm allows and could not be retried with the working prototypes.
claims.quote_verbatim: our executives went up and down Sand Hill Road and burned all of the potential investors
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: Jeri Ellsworth and the demise of CastAR

claims.claim_text: A campaign can function as a volume purchase rather than a funding event: aggregating demand into one order is what allows the product to be priced at its intended level, and the same items sold immediately afterwards in small quantities cost roughly twice as much.
claims.quote_verbatim: the Kickstarter was largely to, to allow us to get down on price
claims.episode_title: Depth and AI with Brandon Gilles and Brian Weinstein

claims.claim_text: A first hardware product committed its makers to about two thousand keyboards with a milled wooden enclosure and individually sculpted keycaps, after visiting roughly a dozen candidate factories and taking bids from half of them.
claims.quote_verbatim: we ended up promising about 2,000 keyboards to Kickstarter backers
claims.speaker: Jesse Vincent
claims.episode_title: Stories from Teardown 2019

claims.claim_text: A single-person project with a ten thousand dollar goal raised about eleven times it, which is the point at which a project becomes a business and the creator inherits the manufacturing problem.
claims.quote_verbatim: we had a goal of 10,000 and I should say I have a goal
claims.speaker: Ken Burns
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ken Burns

claims.claim_text: Paper and cardboard prototypes, the textbook method for validating a product before building it, failed to elicit useful reactions; only a working device assembled from other people's boards, able to make a call and receive a text, produced people asking to buy it. The campaign followed from that reaction rather than preceding it.
claims.quote_verbatim: people wouldn't take me seriously
claims.speaker: Christina Cyr
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Christina Cyr

claims.claim_text: The educational market is reachable for a small hardware vendor provided the administrative burden is accepted, purchase orders included, and provided the product is not otherwise available.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're providing products that they can't get elsewhere, they come to you
claims.speaker: Marcus Schappi
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Marcus Schappi - Kit Ketch Kenophobia

claims.claim_text: A launch structured as a single crescendo, where the product either succeeds or fails on one day, works against the iterative approach that produces good hardware companies. The alternative is shipping something merely good enough early and improving it, rather than perfecting a product before anyone has used it.
claims.quote_verbatim: companies should build, uh, not the perfect product. They should build something quickly that is good enough
claims.speaker: Ben Einstein
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ben Einstein

claims.claim_text: Publicly promised timelines lengthened as the model matured, with one-year delivery dates becoming common where earlier campaigns had promised months.
claims.quote_verbatim: I think a lot of Kickstarters, you see one-year timelines these days
claims.speaker: David Kronstein
claims.episode_title: An Interview with David Kronstein (Tesla500)

claims.claim_text: The test one creator applied before launching was whether he would be confident selling the product in its current state; the answer deferred the campaign until the design was essentially finished, inverting the usual order in which money is raised to fund the remaining development.
claims.quote_verbatim: I was not happy at the state of development. I asked myself, would I be confident in selling this?
claims.episode_title: An Interview with David Kronstein (Tesla500)

claims.claim_text: In the model's early period the platform enforced little, so a campaign could be launched on the strength of being able to make circuit boards, without the accounting of time and cost that the work actually required.
claims.quote_verbatim: I would just like started being like, Oh, I can make some PCBs. Let's do it. Let's do a Kickstarter
claims.speaker: Colin O'Flynn
claims.episode_title: Small Scale Electronics Manufacturing with Colin O'Flynn

claims.claim_text: Presenting off-the-shelf hardware and existing firmware as years of original development is a recurring form of campaign misrepresentation. Reselling a commodity product is a legitimate business; the misrepresentation is in the claimed provenance, including fabricated photographs of development boards.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're just buying it from Alibaba
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Warming Up To IoT - Tendentious Thermal Tools

claims.claim_text: Scale is no protection: the largest European campaign of its time, raising over two million pounds, ended in bankruptcy with backers receiving nothing.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's a, yeah, it is Europe's biggest Kickstarter project
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: 3D Product Logistics

claims.claim_text: Both directions of funding error destroy projects, including those run by established companies: too little to meet the commitment, or so much more than expected that spending expands past what the project can support.
claims.quote_verbatim: either it's not enough as we've talked about to meet their goals, or it's too much and they go wild
